questions.q: Why can't a long-running agent simply rely on 'everything stays in the context window for free'?
options: Because tool_result blocks are never actually added to the conversation
Because the Claude API deletes conversation history automatically after each turn
Because context windows have no size limit at all
Because accumulated history costs real tokens on every subsequent request and can eventually exceed the context window outright
questions.explain: Each iteration's tool_result does go back into context by default, but that accumulation has a real, growing cost and an eventual hard limit, which is exactly why state and memory become a real design concern.

questions.q: What is a 'scratchpad' as a state mechanism, per this lesson?
options: A condensed, explicitly maintained summary of what's been learned so far, shorter than the raw conversation history
A separate, completely unrelated conversation with no connection to the agent's task
A file format that only stores images, never text
A synonym for the Claude API's tools array
questions.explain: A scratchpad applies the same high-signal discipline Lesson 11 used for tool output, now applied to an entire session's accumulated state — keeping only what's actually needed, condensed.

questions.q: What does Anthropic's memory tool let Claude do, and what family of tools does it belong to?
options: It deletes all prior conversation history permanently; it is unrelated to any other tool
It lets Claude store and retrieve information across conversations in files it controls, and belongs to the same family as the bash and text editor tools
It is a server tool that requires no application code to execute at all
It replaces the need for the tool_use/tool_result mechanism entirely with a new protocol
questions.explain: The memory tool is an Anthropic-schema client tool, in the same family as bash and the text editor tool — your application still executes the real file operations via the same tool_use/tool_result round trip.

questions.q: What do ReAct's Thought/Action/Observation history, a planning agent's revised plan, an orchestrator's collected worker results, and a reflection loop's draft/feedback cycles all have in common, per this lesson?
options: None of them produce any state that needs to be stored anywhere
They can only ever be stored using the memory tool specifically, with no other option
They are all identical mechanisms with no meaningful differences
Each is a form of accumulated state that has to go somewhere — conversation history, a scratchpad, or external memory, depending on the need
questions.explain: Every pattern from this chapter generates state, and none of those patterns themselves specify where that state should live — this lesson's three mechanisms are the real answers to that separate question.

questions.q: What determines which of the three memory mechanisms (conversation history, scratchpad, external memory) is the right choice for a given agent's accumulated state?
options: The programming language the agent happens to be written in
How long the state needs to persist and how much of it needs to stay immediately accessible versus retrieved on demand
Whether the agent has ever called a tool named 'get_weather'
The mechanism is always the same regardless of the situation
questions.explain: The three mechanisms trade off differently on persistence and accessibility — the right choice depends on the actual shape of the task's state needs, not a one-size-fits-all default.
